sourceText: Aster did not announce the night’s theme. She opened the CULTURE-CONTACT-TRIBUNAL sector and let the children discover for themselves which of the world’s rules concerned them directly. A post-scarcity civilization can stop an empire's atrocities but cannot guarantee what order will follow. The memorial bore the name of Iain M. Banks precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. The children discovered that technology often solves the problem it can measure and moves the conflict into a variable it never measured. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. At the center of the conflict was Darin, an administrator chosen precisely because they were not a specialist in the phenomenon that had reorganized the world. ‘The specialists tell me what can be done,’ they said. ‘I have to answer who it may be done to.’ Kesh kept the distinction in his notes. 227 The problem closed quickly around them: The victims themselves want incompatible things: some ask for intervention, while others fear it will delegitimize local resistance. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Ps — Post-Scarcity: material goods become nearly free; Ag — AI Governance: artificial intelligences administer institutions; Mf — Multispecies Federation: different species share institutions. Course references included Iain M. Banks — Culture; Culture and AI governance; pluralist SF. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Kesh broke the first consensus. ‘If the element explains everything, we do not have an element. We have a word that has eaten the problem.’ Vela answered without raising their voice: ‘If we can save the situation only by making the world resemble us more closely, we have not demonstrated the superiority of our solution. We have demonstrated only our power.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated 228 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. The children vote differently, and Aster preserves the minority position as part of the decision rather than treating it as an error to be eliminated. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the OUTFINITE operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — allows successive finite extensions without postulating an already-given final infinite state — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of 229 a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 230 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
